wine.name: El Grifo Malvasía Volcánica Seco Colección
wine.grapes: Malvasía Volcánica alone, Lanzarote's own white grape, by the usual account a natural crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo.
wine.sites: Ungrafted vines of forty to sixty years, by the house's account, each planted in a pit dug through the black volcanic ash that covers much of Lanzarote, down to the older soil beneath.
wine.making: By the house's own sheets, the grapes are picked by hand into small crates from late July, as each part of the island ripens, and the must is settled and fermented with the house's own yeast, selected from its vineyards. The wine is bottled young, to keep the perfume of the grape.
wine.glass: Orange blossom and jasmine on the nose, moving towards apricot; dry and light on its feet, with fresh, balanced acidity and a saline finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, while its blossom and apricot are fresh; for a fuller Malvasía Volcánica, the house bottles Lías, kept some seven months on its stirred lees.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass, with grilled fish or the island's goat's cheese.

label.means: Lanzarote's own white grape, grown in pits dug through the island's volcanic ash.
Dry: the house also makes a semi-sweet Malvasía of the same range and sweet Malvasías.
The house's name for this range, which holds the dry and the semi-sweet Malvasía.

records.table: El Grifo's Malvasía Volcánica Seco Colección is a dry white of Lanzarote's own grape, from ungrafted vines in pits dug through black volcanic ash, bottled young. It smells of orange blossom and apricot and ends saline: pour it cold with grilled fish.
records.story: Between 1730 and 1736 the eruptions of Timanfaya buried much of Lanzarote's farmland under lava and black lapilli, the picón. Growers learnt to dig through it to the old soil, planting each vine in a pit behind a low wall of stone, and the vine landscape of La Geria grew out of that labour. In 1775, by the founding inscription the house keeps, a priest of the parish church of Teguise built the covered press house at El Grifo, which the house counts as the oldest winery of the Canaries and among the ten oldest in Spain. Three families have held it since, by the house's account, the third from the 1880s. The Lanzarote artist César Manrique (1919 to 1992), a friend of the family, urged it to keep the old press house when a new winery was built beside it in the 1980s; restored on his advice, it opened as a museum of wine, and the griffin he drew marks the house's bottles. El Grifo marked its 250th year in 2025. Its dry Malvasía Volcánica is the plainest statement of the island's grape and of what the pits give: a fresh, perfumed white from vines that phylloxera never reached.

traps: Malvasía Volcánica is Lanzarote's own grape, not the Malvasia of Madeira or of Italy, and the Seco Colección is dry, not the sweet Canary of history.
The pits of La Geria are dug through volcanic lapilli, the picón of the eruptions of the 1730s, not through sand or chalk.

questions.q: A guest asks how the vines behind El Grifo's Malvasía Volcánica Seco Colección are planted. Which answer fits?

A bishop of the Canary Islands
questions.exp: César Manrique (1919 to 1992), a friend of the family, drew the griffin and urged the house to keep its press house of 1775; a priest of Teguise, not a bishop, had built it.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35; the one fetch of the run was tried on elgrifo.com and refused, so the house's pages were read through search summaries only.

1775 is the house's date for its covered press house, from the founding inscription, and stands also on Vinetur, La Voz de Lanzarote and the Lanzarote Guidebook; the oldest winery of the Canaries and one of the ten oldest of Spain are hedged as the house's claim, as the plan's note asks.
The builder of 1775 is named on the house's page with his dates (1725 to 1807), but on no second source read, so the story describes him as a priest of the parish church of Teguise.

Ungrafted vines of forty to sixty years, the day's chilling, the house yeast and the 16 degrees until bottling are from the house's own sheets of the 2022 and 2024 vintages; no sheet read mentions oak or a time on lees for the Seco, so the record says neither.

The new winery beside the press house is dated 1981 by one account and the museum's restoration 1986 by the house's museum page (1984 by its timeline), so the story says the 1980s; the griffin as the house's emblem since 1990 rests on the joint announcement of the house and the Fundación César Manrique, and Manrique's authorship of it on the house and Gazette Life.

The sale of 1880 to a named family rests on one source (lanzarote.com) and is left out; the house's present owners and its oenologist are living and are not named (names met, for people.json: the two Otamendi brothers, Juan José and Fermín, and the oenologist Jorge Rodríguez).
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; the region record's producers line (a house of the eighteenth century with a wine museum) agrees. No swap proposed.

changed: wine.making: "By the house's own sheet, the grapes are picked from late July as each part of the island ripens and chilled for a day; the must is then settled and ..." now "By the house's own sheets, the grapes are picked by hand into small crates from late July, as each part of the island ripens, and the must is settled and ...": Two searches found no sheet of the Seco with the 16 degrees, the cloudy holding or the chilling; the house's own yeast and the settling stand on its Lías sheet of 2022, and the hand harvest at the end of July on its Semidulce sheets, made together with the Seco.

wine.ageing: "for a Malvasía Volcánica made to keep, the house bottles Lías, aged a year on its lees." now "for a fuller Malvasía Volcánica, the house bottles Lías, kept some seven months on its stirred lees.": The house's Lías page and the importer's sheet give seven months with the lees in suspension and bâtonnage, part in French oak; no source read calls it made to keep.

others[0].note: "Malvasía Volcánica kept a year in tank on its fine lees and stirred: the house's dry white made to keep." now "Malvasía Volcánica kept about seven months on its stirred lees, mostly in tank with a part in French oak, by the house's sheet of 2022.": As above: seven months, 30 per cent in 500 litre French oak barrels and the rest in tank.

story: "It has passed through three families since." now "Three families have held it since, by the house's account, the third from the 1880s.": The house's history counts three families in all, the founder's among them; the buyer of the third is dated 1880 on one line of the page and 1886 on another, so the decade is given.

story: "and the griffin he drew has marked the house's bottles since 1990, by the house's account." now "and the griffin he drew marks the house's bottles.": The griffin is Manrique's on the house's page and Gazette Life; no year for it was found in two searches (1990 and 1991 are the last stages of the old winery's restoration, and 1986 a painting for a label).

wine.label[3].means: "The island's own appellation for its Malvasía, Listán and Moscatel." now "The island's own appellation, named for Lanzarote.": A label term needs no list of grapes, and the DO's full list was not tested, so the narrower wording is taken out rather than left to imply a limit.
open: The age of the vines: forty to sixty years on Vinissimus and the house's sheets as the author read them, forty to fifty on the house's shop page for 2023.
Whether the Seco ever sees oak or lees: no sheet read says so either way, and the record says neither.
The year of the griffin as the house's emblem: not found; the old winery's restoration is dated 1986 to 1991 by the house.

wine.name: Bermejo Malvasía Seco
wine.grapes: Malvasía Volcánica alone, Lanzarote's own white grape, by the usual account a crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo, also called Bermejuela.
wine.sites: Malvasía Volcánica grown on Lanzarote, each low vine set in a pit dug through the volcanic crust to the older soil beneath and sheltered from the wind by a wall of stone.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in tank, by the importer's and the merchants' sheets, and bottled young without oak. The house makes a separate Malvasía fermented and aged on its lees in French oak barrels; this is the plain dry white of the range.
wine.glass: Ripe lemon and juicy mango, then a subtle trace of wildflowers; dry and light, with the lively acidity Malvasía Volcánica keeps on Lanzarote's ash.
wine.ageing: Bottled young and made to be drunk young, while its lemon and mango are fresh; it is not a white for long keeping.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass, with grilled fish or papas arrugadas with mojo sauce.

records.table: Los Bermejos, at La Florida on Lanzarote, makes Bermejo Malvasía Seco from Malvasía Volcánica grown in pits dug through the island's ash, made in tank and bottled young without oak. It smells of ripe lemon and mango with a hint of wildflowers; pour it cold.
records.story: Lanzarote's vineyards were remade by fire. The eruptions of 1730 to 1736 buried much of the island's farmland under lapilli, and growers learnt to dig through it, planting each vine at the bottom of a pit behind a wall of stone, where the vine shelters from the wind. The Malvasía grown there came to the Canaries in the sixteenth century, by the house's account from Madeira, and on the island's ash it became a grape of its own, Malvasía Volcánica. Los Bermejos takes its name from its estate at La Florida, in San Bartolomé, where an older bodega had worked for generations. By 2001 it had all but stopped, and that year a new company took it over to bring it back to life, by the account of the island's denomination. The revived house works across the island's styles: dry, semi-sweet and naturally sweet Malvasía, a sparkling Malvasía aged on its lees by the traditional method, a Malvasía fermented in barrel, Listán Negro and sweet Moscatel. Its dry Malvasía, made in tank and bottled young, is the plainest way to taste the grape the pits were dug for.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35, with the DO Lanzarote's order and the eruptions shared with El Grifo; no fetch tried on this house.

Founded is left empty, as the plan's note asks: 2001 is the founding for Vinissimus and a relaunch for Lonely Planet, and the DO Lanzarote's own page says a new company took control in 2001 to revive an older bodega, which the story follows; Diario de Avisos says the bodega had worked for centuries on the estate, so the story says for generations.

The label: Spanish merchants (Decantalo, Vinissimus) list the wine as Bermejo Malvasía Seco, while the American importer and its merchants print Los Bermejos Malvasía Volcánica Seco; the checker should confirm the words on a current Spanish bottle.

The making rests on secondary sheets only: tank aged for the importer, fermented and aged in stainless steel for Astor Wines, aged on its fine lees and not clarified for Decantalo; the lees is left out for want of a second source, and no sheet of the house's own for the Seco was found.

The glass rests on merchants' notes (Flatiron Wines: ripe lemon, juicy mango, wildflowers; Spanish Wine Lover: fruity and floral); the ageing is the style's, a tank made young white, with no source of its own.

The house's page says Malvasía came from Madeira in the sixteenth century and mutated on the island into a distinct clone, while the region record and the merchants call Malvasía Volcánica a crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo; the record keeps the crossing, and the clone is reported here as a tension.
The owner and winemaker is living and not named (for people.json: Ignacio Valdera). Vinissimus's figure of the share of grapes the estate grows is volatile and left out.

No swap proposed: Spanish Wine Lover calls the dry Malvasía the house's flagship, so the pick stands, though El Grifo's flagship is also a dry Malvasía Volcánica; the plan's alternative, the Listán Negro rosado, is left to the checker.

wine.name: Suertes del Marqués 7 Fuentes
wine.grapes: Listán Negro, the great majority, with a little Tintilla, given as Castellana Negra on the house's own sheet of 2021.
wine.sites: Many plots of the estate and of local growers, all within the municipality of La Orotava: about twenty on the house's sheet of 2021, more on others. The vines are ungrafted, of about ten to 180 years, many braided in cordón trenzado, at about 350 to 750 metres.
wine.making: Each plot is fermented apart, in small concrete vats, and the lots are blended only shortly before bottling. The wine is aged for eight to eleven months by the sheets of different vintages, partly in concrete and partly in used French oak, 500 litre barrels and larger casks, to round it rather than to give it the taste of oak.
wine.glass: Cherry, wild raspberry and cracked black pepper over dried roses and wet pumice; fresh and long, with a saline finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fresh on release, it is made to be drunk over its first few years rather than laid down for decades.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass, with grilled meat, tuna or rabbit.

label.means: The wine's name, Spanish for seven springs: the house's village red, blended from many plots.
The valley's appellation on Tenerife's north coast below Teide, its rules ratified in Madrid in 1995.
Red: the house makes whites of Listán Blanco beside it.

records.table: Suertes del Marqués makes 7 Fuentes in the Orotava valley on Tenerife: Listán Negro from many plots of old, ungrafted vines, many braided into cordón trenzado. It is fresh and peppery, with cherry, dried roses and a saline finish; pour it a little cool.
records.story: Tenerife's Orotava valley runs down from Teide to the north coast, and its growers train their vines in the cordón trenzado, braiding several long canes into a rope held off the ground on props. Suerte is an old Spanish word for a small plot of farmland, above all one received by inheritance. The family behind Suertes del Marqués grew grapes in the valley for some twenty years and sold them to other wineries before it began to make wine of its own in 2006, by its own account. The valley's denomination, approved by the Canary government in December 1994, was ratified by an order of 15 November 1995. The house works plot by plot, fermenting each apart in concrete and ageing in large casks, and it bottles a village wine of many plots beside wines of single plots. 7 Fuentes is the village wine: many plots of Listán Negro, ungrafted, some of the vines well over a century old, with a little Tintilla or Castellana Negra. For a sommelier it is the wine to open first when a guest asks what the valley's old braided vines give: a peppery red of freshness rather than weight.

others.name: Suertes del Marqués Vidonia
others.note: The house's white of Listán Blanco from old vines in the valley.

traps: 7 Fuentes is a village wine blended from many plots, not a single vineyard; the house's single plot reds, such as La Solana and El Esquilón, carry their own names.
Listán Negro is a black grape of its own, not a dark form of Listán Blanco, which is Palomino.

cards.front: How is 7 Fuentes made from its many plots?

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, with the DO's order shared with Envínate; no fetch tried on this house.

2006 is the house's own date (its winery page: making wine since 2006, growers for twenty years before, selling grapes to other wineries of the appellation), borne out by Vinissimus; the founders are a father and his sons, and the son who leads the house is living, so nobody is named (for people.json: Jonatan García Lima; the father, Francisco Javier García Núñez, of unknown status, as a precaution).

The plan's note says Listán Negro with Tintilla; the house's own sheet for 2021 gives Listán Negro with Castellana Negra (97 and 3), Enterwine 95 and 5, and Bodeboca's 2015 page 90 Listán Negro and 10 Tintilla, which it equates with Castellana Negra; the record follows the house and leaves Tintilla to the checker.

The twenty plots, the vines of ten to 180 years, the separate fermentation and the eleven months in foudre and barrel are the house's sheet of 2021; Enterwine gives eleven months in concrete and French oak, Bodeboca twenty five vineyards and 350 to 700 metres, so the record keeps the house's figures and says about.

Retailers label the wine Vino de Villa, Valle de la Orotava (Enterwine, Leon and Son), which may be the house's own tier word; with the source cap reached it is left off the label and named here for the checker.

The meaning of suertes rests on Indigo Wine and Gourmet Hunters; Gourmet Hunters' landlord whose name was added, and Indigo's inheritance laws, are each on one source and left out. The glass rests on two critics' published notes (black pepper, dried roses, wet pumice; cherry, wild raspberry, cracked peppercorn, saline), the critics living and unnamed; the ageing is the style's, with no source of its own.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; the region record's producers line agrees. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Envínate Benje Tinto
wine.grapes: Listán Prieto, the great majority, with a little Tintilla and, in some vintages, some Listán Blanco.
wine.sites: Old, ungrafted bush vines on the volcanic slopes of Santiago del Teide in the west of Tenerife, at about 1,000 metres.
wine.making: By the importer's sheets, each parcel is fermented apart in concrete tanks or small open tubs, for ten to twenty days with a daily punching down. The wine is pressed into old French barriques for its malolactic and aged there on its fine lees for about eight months, without stirring, and bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Dried rose petals, black pepper and a smoky note like gunpowder over wet basalt; light in body and savoury, with tart, crunchy fruit, a salty edge and lively acidity.
wine.ageing: Lively on release and good within its first years; a young bottle can be reductive when first opened and opens with time in the glass.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The red of the Benje range; Benje Blanco is the white from the same high vineyards.

records.table: Envínate's Benje Tinto comes from old, ungrafted Listán Prieto at about 1,000 metres on the western slopes of Tenerife, fermented in concrete and aged eight months in old barrels. Pale and peppery, with dried roses, smoke and wet stone, it wants a cool pour and a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Envínate began in 2005, when four friends who had met studying oenology at the Miguel Hernández University in the province of Alicante finished their studies and set up a consultancy together; making wines of their own became the second half of the work. They went looking for old vineyards and found them in several places, among them the Ribeira Sacra in Galicia, Almansa and Tenerife, where phylloxera never arrived and the vines grow on their own roots. On the island they made two ranges: Táganan, from the Anaga hills of the north-east, and Benje, from high vineyards around Santiago del Teide in the west, sold under the Ycoden-Daute-Isora denomination, recognised in 1994. Their way is the same in each place: each parcel fermented apart, concrete and old barrels rather than new oak, and no filtering. Benje Tinto is mostly Listán Prieto, the grape known in the Americas as País and as the Mission grape, here from old bush vines at about 1,000 metres. For a sommelier it is the Tenerife red to set beside the island's Listán Negro: paler, more peppery and savoury, and from a different grape.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35; no site of the group's own was found, so the wine rests on the American and British importers' sheets (José Pastor Selections and Indigo Wine, which copy the producer's own sheets) and on merchants, with no primary source but the denomination's order.

2005 stands on Primal Wine, Lay Wheeler and Pearl of Burgundy (four friends who met studying oenology at the Miguel Hernández University in Elche, a consultancy formed on graduating); one account puts the first wines in about 2008, which is left out for want of a second.

The blend moves by vintage: 95 Listán Prieto and 5 Tintilla on one sheet, 96, 2 and 2 with Listán Blanco on the sheet of 2020, about 90, 9 and 1 for 2023 and 2024; one merchant lists Graciano and another Listán Negro alone, which the record does not follow.

The sheet of 2020 gives vines of 70 to 120 years at 75 to 300 metres, which fits Táganan rather than Benje, against about 1,000 metres on every other source, so the record keeps 1,000 metres and gives no age for the vines; native yeasts are stated on the sheets of Benje Blanco and Táganan, not of Benje Tinto, so the record does not claim them.

The four founders are living and never named (for people.json: Roberto Santana, Alfonso Torrente, Laura Ramos, José Martínez); one source says a founder consulted for Suertes del Marqués, which is left out for want of a second. Benje's place inside the DO Ycoden-Daute-Isora rests on merchants' labels (Decantalo, Mister Meister), since the order's list of municipalities was not read.

The glass rests on critics' and merchants' notes of several vintages (wet basalt, dried rose petals, black pepper, gunpowder; smoky, crunchy, salty, peppery, reductive at first); the critics are living and unnamed, and the ageing follows the note that a young bottle opens with patience.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record, which the integrator may wish to add to the producers line. No swap proposed: the record is about the Tenerife wine, as the plan's note asks.

changed: wine.making: "Each parcel is fermented apart in concrete tanks or small open tubs, partly with whole bunches, for ten to twenty days with a daily punching down." now "By the importer's sheets, each parcel is fermented apart in concrete tanks or small open tubs, for ten to twenty days with a daily punching down.": Whole bunches appear on the sheet of 2020 alone, against destemmed fruit on the others; the making is hedged as the importer's sheets.
story: "each parcel fermented apart, whole bunches in part, concrete and old barrels" now "each parcel fermented apart, concrete and old barrels": As above.

story, cards[0].back and questions[1].exp: "the Miguel Hernández University in Elche; at Elche" now "the Miguel Hernández University in the province of Alicante; at the Miguel Hernández University": Every account read places the four at the university in Alicante; the university's seat is Elche but none of the sources puts the oenology course there.

wine.name: Teneguía Malvasía Aromática Dulce
wine.grapes: Malvasía Aromática alone, the old Malvasía of the sweet Canary wine.
wine.sites: Growers' vineyards around Fuencaliente, at the volcanic southern tip of La Palma, where the vines grow ungrafted in black volcanic ash.
wine.making: Under the DO La Palma's rules a Malvasía Dulce comes from overripe Malvasía, picked late by the island's traditional methods, and keeps at least 45 grams of sugar per litre. Its sweetness is the grape's own: no spirit is added.
wine.glass: Honey, candied apricot and beeswax, the notes of La Palma's sweet Malvasía; sweet, but held by fresh acidity, with a long, lingering finish.
wine.ageing: Good young for its perfume, while its sugar and fresh acidity let a sound bottle keep for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a small white wine glass, with almond sweets or blue cheese.

label.means: The old Malvasía of the sweet Canary wine, grown above all at Fuencaliente.
Sweet: under the DO's rules, at least 45 grams of sugar per litre, from overripe grapes.
The island's appellation, with Fuencaliente one of its three subzones.

records.table: Bodegas Teneguía is the winery of Llanovid, the growers' co-operative of Fuencaliente on La Palma, and its Malvasía Aromática Dulce comes from overripe grapes on the volcanic south of the island. Honeyed yet fresh, it is an heir to the sweet Canary of history; pour it cold.
records.story: Malvasía has grown on La Palma since the sixteenth century: the island's denomination holds a lease of 27 September 1555 for a vineyard of Malvasía, and the sweet Malvasía of the Canaries became the wine England knew as Canary. Fuencaliente, at the island's southern tip, grows most of the Malvasía that goes into the island's sweet wine, in black volcanic ash. The winery at Fuencaliente dates from the 1940s, 1945 by some accounts and 1947 by others; it works as a co-operative of growers, Llanovid, whose wines carry the Teneguía name. Teneguía is also the name of the volcano that erupted south of the town from 26 October to 18 November 1971, among lavas left by an older eruption of 1677. The co-operative's sweet Malvasía Aromática, made from grapes left to overripen on the vine and sweet with their own sugar, is the bottle that carries Fuencaliente's tradition to a guest's table. For a sommelier it is the place to start on the sweet Canary of history: not fortified, not Madeira, but a sweet white of overripe Malvasía from volcanic ash.

La Palma's Malvasía Aromática is not Lanzarote's Malvasía Volcánica, and its Dulce is sweet from overripe grapes, not fortified with spirit.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35; no site of the co-operative's own was found, so the wine rests on the DO La Palma's own pages and rules, read through search, and no technical sheet of this bottling was read.

Founded is left empty, as the plan's note allows: 1947 stands on Spanish Wine Lover and Lonely Planet, 1945 on two others (a winery built in 1945, established in 1945), and a business register gives Llanovid's constitution as 1989, which is likely a later registration; the story says the 1940s and gives both years.

The co-operative's name Llanovid and the brands Teneguía and Llanos Negros are on the DO La Palma's own list of makers of Malvasía Dulce and on the Starlight article; the label words Malvasía Aromática Dulce follow the plan and VINESPAÑA's medal of 2024 for a Teneguía Malvasía Aromática naturalmente dulce, which the checker should confirm on a bottle.

The making is the DO's rule for a Malvasía Dulce (overripe grapes, late picking, more than 45 grams of sugar per litre), with the sweetness the grape's own on two accounts of La Palma's sweet Malvasía; the co-operative's vessels and time in tank or wood were not found and are left out. The glass is the style's as sources describe La Palma's sweet Malvasías (honey, dried and candied apricot, beeswax, citrus, sweetness held by acidity), since no note of this bottling was found; the checker should look for one.

Estelar, the long aged bottling the plan names, rests on one guide (180 months in oak, botrytis lots) and is left out of others; the co-operative's winemaker is living and not named (for people.json: Carlos Lozano).

Tension with the region record: it puts Fuencaliente's sweet Malvasía on the ash of the San Antonio eruption of 1677, while the DO La Palma's page calls the San Antonio volcano prehispanic and the 1677 lavas are those of the Fuencaliente eruption; the record says only an older eruption of 1677. The year 1677 for the older eruption rests on Wikipedia's article on Teneguía beside the region record. The DO's order of 16 February 1994 and the recovery of vineyards from that year are on the Consejo's own history page, left out of the record for the source cap.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; the region record's producers line agrees. No swap proposed; the record says plainly that it is a co-operative, as the note asks.

changed: wine.making, wine.label[1].means and cards[1].back: "more than 45 grams of sugar per litre" now "at least 45 grams of sugar per litre": The pliego of 2011 sets sweet wines at 45 grams as a minimum; more than 45 is the Canary rule of 2003.

wine.glass: "Honey and dried apricot with orange peel and a touch of beeswax; sweet, but held by fresh acidity, with a long, lingering finish." now "Honey, candied apricot and beeswax, the notes of La Palma's sweet Malvasía; sweet, but held by fresh acidity, with a long, lingering finish.": No note of this bottling was found; the notes are the style's, as another maker's sweet Malvasía Aromática of La Palma is described, and orange peel is on no source read.

table: "it is the old sweet Canary in a modern bottle" now "it is an heir to the sweet Canary of history": A modern Malvasía Dulce is not the Canary of the seventeenth century; the plan's why calls it the heir the region record names. A wording change, with no new fact.
